questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?
questions.title: Class vs Object in Java
questions.direct_answer: A class declares a type's fields, constructors, and methods. An object is a runtime instance of a class with its own instance-field state. One class can have many objects; static members are associated with the loaded class rather than copied into each object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that a class is a template and an object is a live instance — and that each object has its own independent data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'class' and 'object' interchangeably, or thinking all objects share the same field values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the class declares the instance fields and behavior, but each object allocates its own heap memory at runtime — and only static fields are shared.

sections.title: A Class Is the Blueprint; an Object Is the Thing You Build From It
sections.content:
A **class** declares a Java type: its fields, constructors, and methods. An **object** is one runtime instance of that class. If `Student` declares `name` and `marks`, two `Student` objects can hold different values while using the behavior declared by the same class.

`Student s;` declares a variable but does not create a `Student`; a local variable must be assigned before use. `Student s = new Student(...)` creates an instance and makes `s` refer to it. Assigning `Student other = s` copies the reference, not the object's fields, so both variables then refer to the same instance.

Do not say a class 'uses no memory.' When loaded, the JVM keeps class metadata and a `Class` object, and static fields are associated with that loaded class. The beginner-level distinction is simply type declaration versus runtime instance.

sections.title: One Class, Many Independent Objects
sections.content:
When you call `new` three times on the same class, three separate objects appear on the heap — each at its own address, each with its own field values. ```mermaid flowchart TD C["Student class
(type declaration)"] -->|"new Student()"| O1["s1 @ heap 0x100
name: Alice, marks: 95"] C -->|"new Student()"| O2["s2 @ heap 0x200
name: Bob, marks: 72"] C -->|"new Student()"| O3["s3 @ heap 0x300
name: Carol, marks: 88"] O1 -.->|"changing s1.marks
does NOT affect"| O2 ``` The class itself never appears on the heap — only the objects do. Each one is independent.

sections.title: Class and Objects in Practice
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using "class" and "object" as if they mean the same thing** — the class is the definition you write, the object is one live instance built from it; the interviewer hears the slip the moment you make it.
- **Assuming all objects of a class share their field values** — each object gets its own copy of the instance fields, so changing `s1.marks` never touches `s2.marks` unless that field is `static`.
- **Believing `Student s;` already creates an object** — it only creates a `null` reference; the object exists only after `new`, and touching `s` before that throws `NullPointerException`.
- **Thinking the class takes heap memory** — only objects live on the heap; the class is loaded once as a template, so "how many objects" and "how many classes" are completely different questions.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Class**: declares a type's data shape and behavior.
- **Object**: one runtime instance with its own instance fields.
- **Declaration is not construction**: `Student s;` creates no Student object.
- **`new`**: creates an instance and returns a reference to it.
- **Static members**: associated with the loaded class, not copied into every object.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A class is the declaration of a type—its fields, constructors, and methods. An object is one runtime instance of that class. One Student class can therefore have many Student objects, each with different name and marks values.

Declaring `Student s` does not create an object. After `s = new Student(...)`, the variable refers to an instance. If I then write `Student other = s`, Java copies the reference, so there is still one object and changes through either reference are visible through the other.

questions.question: What happens in memory when you create an object using the `new` keyword in Java?
questions.title: What `new` Does in Memory
questions.direct_answer: Evaluating `new Student(...)` creates a new object, initializes its instance fields to default values, runs the selected constructor (including the superclass constructor chain), and produces a reference to the object. The Java language does not expose the object's numeric address or require the local reference to occupy a particular stack location.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the difference between stack (reference) and heap (object data), and the 4-step sequence that new triggers.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the object lives on the stack, or that the variable and the object are the same thing. The variable is just a reference; the object is on the heap.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that every object carries a hidden object header (metadata used by the JVM for garbage collection and type identification), so the actual memory footprint is slightly larger than just the fields.

sections.title: The Four Things `new` Does Every Time You Call It
sections.content:
When Java evaluates `new Student(...)`, it creates a fresh object and returns a reference to it. Before the body of `Student`'s constructor runs, the object's instance fields have their default values. Constructor execution follows the constructor chain: superclass initialization happens before the subclass constructor body completes. Field initializers and instance initializer blocks also run in the order defined by Java.

The selected constructor then establishes the object's intended starting state. When the expression finishes, its result is a reference that can be assigned, passed, or returned. Two variables may later hold references to the same object; assigning one reference to another does not clone the object.

A JVM normally manages objects in heap storage, but the Java language does not expose raw object addresses or require one physical placement. Optimizing JVMs may use escape analysis while preserving exactly the same observable reference behavior. Explain the language semantics rather than promising a four-step physical memory layout.

sections.title: The 4-Step Sequence Every Time `new` Runs
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["new Student(name, marks)"] --> B["Create a fresh Student object"]
    B --> C["Fields receive default values"]
    C --> D["Run superclass and instance initialization"]
    D --> E["Run the selected constructor body"]
    E --> F["Expression produces a reference to the object"]
```

sections.title: Stack vs Heap After `Student s1 = new Student()`
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR S1["Student s1"] --> O["one Student object
name: Alice
marks: 95"] S2["Student s2 = s1"] --> O N["s1 = null"] -. "changes only s1" .-> X["no reference"] ``` After `s2 = s1`, both variables refer to one object. Setting one variable to `null` does not destroy an object still reachable through the other.

sections.title: Watching the Four Steps — Default Fill, Then the Constructor
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the object lives on the stack** — only the reference (the address) sits on the stack; the actual object data always lives on the heap, and confusing the two is the single most common error here.
- **Believing the constructor creates the object** — heap allocation and default-filling happen first; by the time the constructor runs the object already exists, and the constructor only sets its initial values.
- **Assuming `s1 = null` deletes the object** — it just removes one reference; the object survives on the heap until no reference points to it and the garbage collector reclaims it.
- **Reading `Student s2 = s1` as a copy** — it copies the address, not the object, so both variables drive the same heap object and a change through one is visible through the other.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`new` creates a fresh object** and produces a reference.
- **Fields begin with defaults** before explicit initialization completes.
- **Constructor chain**: superclass construction and instance initialization follow Java's defined order.
- **Constructor establishes state**; it is part of object creation, not a separate factory.
- **No raw address model**: Java specifies reference behavior, not a stack/heap diagram as a language guarantee.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`new Student("Asha")` creates a new `Student` object, gives its fields their default values, performs superclass and instance initialization in Java's defined order, and then runs the selected constructor. The result of the expression is a reference to that object, which can be stored in a variable such as `Student first`.

For example, after `Student second = first`, Java has not copied the `Student`; both variables refer to the same object. Changing `second.name` is therefore visible through `first`. Reassigning `second` to another object does not change what `first` refers to. Exact placement and raw addresses are JVM implementation details, so the portable explanation is about object creation, initialization, and reference values rather than a promised stack-versus-heap diagram.

questions.question: What is the difference between a reference variable and the object it points to in Java?
questions.title: Reference Variable vs Object in Java
questions.direct_answer: A reference variable holds either `null` or a reference to an object; it is not the object itself and Java does not expose it as a raw address. Several variables can refer to the same object, so a mutation through one reference is visible through the others. `==` tests reference identity, while `equals()` tests the equality policy defined by the class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that a variable is not the object — it is a reference — and can reason about what happens when two variables point to the same object.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `Student s1 = new Student()` as though `s1` IS the student. s1 is just the address. The real student data is on the heap.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the two-variable-same-object scenario: `s2 = s1` means both variables point to the same heap object. Changing one changes what the other sees — there is no copy.

sections.title: The Remote Control and the TV: Why the Variable Isn't the Object
sections.content:
A variable of class type does not contain the object's fields. It holds a **reference** or `null`. `Student s1 = new Student()` creates an object and makes `s1` refer to it. `Student s2 = s1` copies the reference value, so `s1` and `s2` are separate variables that reach the same object.

Changing `s2.marks` changes that shared object's state, which is why `s1.marks` sees the result. Reassigning `s2` does not reassign `s1`. If a reference is `null`, trying to use it to access an instance member throws `NullPointerException`.

Java references are not C pointers: source code cannot perform address arithmetic or inspect a portable numeric address. `s1 == s2` asks whether the references denote the same object. `s1.equals(s2)` follows the equality behavior implemented by the class.

sections.title: Two References, One Object — and a Null Reference
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR S1["s1"] --> O["one Student object
name: Alice
marks: 95"] S2["s2 = s1"] --> O S3["s3 = null"] -.-> N["no object"] ``` `s1` and `s2` are different variables referring to one object; `s3` refers to no object.

sections.title: Two References to One Object — Proof
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the variable as the object** — `s1` is only the address; the real Student data lives on the heap, and saying "`s1` is the student" hides every bug that comes from sharing.
- **Expecting `s2 = s1` to make a copy** — it copies the reference, so both variables point at one object; modifying through `s2` is instantly visible through `s1`.
- **Comparing objects with `==`** — `==` checks whether two references hold the same object, not whether the objects have equal content; use `.equals()` for content, and two separate `new` objects are `==` false even with identical fields.
- **Calling a method on a `null` reference** — `s3.name` when `s3` is `null` throws `NullPointerException`; a declared reference is not an object until something is assigned to it.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Reference variable**: holds an object reference or `null`; it is not the object.
- **Assignment copies the reference**: it does not clone the object.
- **Aliasing**: two references can reach one mutable object.
- **`null`**: no object; dereferencing it throws `NullPointerException`.
- **`==` versus `equals`**: identity versus the class's logical-equality rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A reference variable holds a reference to an object or null; it is not the object itself. If `s2 = s1`, Java copies the reference, so both variables refer to the same Student. A field change through one is then visible through the other, while reassigning one variable leaves the other unchanged.

`==` on references tests whether they denote the same object. `equals()` can define value equality. I avoid calling the reference a reference identity or pointer because Java exposes reference semantics, not portable address values or pointer arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance members and static members in a Java class?
questions.title: Instance Members vs Static Members in Java
questions.direct_answer: Instance fields belong to individual objects, and instance methods run with a `this` reference. Static members are associated with a loaded class and can be used without an instance; a static method has no `this`. A static field is shared by instances of that particular loaded class, so class loaders matter in advanced applications.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that instance members are per-object and static members are per-class, and know when to use each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using static for fields that should vary per object — e.g. making `name` static means all Students suddenly share one name. Also trying to access instance members from a static method (compile error).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the classic static counter example: `static int count` incremented in the constructor gives you the total number of objects ever created, shared across all instances.

sections.title: Per-Object vs Per-Class: Who Owns the Data
sections.content:
An **instance member** belongs to each object separately, and a **static member** belongs to the class as a whole. The whole difference comes down to one question: who owns this piece of data?

Why have both? Some data is personal to each object — one student's `name` and `marks` have nothing to do with another's. But some data belongs to the type itself — like a running count of how many students have ever been created. You don't want that count copied into every object; you want one shared number. **That's exactly the line between instance and static.**

Here is how it works. **Instance members** are fields and methods written *without* the `static` keyword. Every object gets its own copy, so `s1.name` and `s2.name` are completely separate boxes. **Static members** are written *with* `static`, and there is exactly one value per loaded class, shared by every object — you can even use it before any object exists, by writing `Student.count`. A good way to picture it: instance fields are like each student's own notebook, while a static field is a single whiteboard on the classroom wall that everyone reads and writes.

The classic interview move is the **static counter**: put `static int count = 0` in the class and write `count++` inside the constructor. Because the field is shared, every `new` bumps the same number — so `Student.count` tells you how many objects were ever created.

The gotcha that produces a compile error: **a static method cannot directly touch instance fields** or instance methods. A static method runs without any object, so there is no `this` — and if you reference `name` inside it, the compiler asks "which object's `name`?" and there is no answer.

> **Remember:** instance members are per-object (own copy); `static` members are per-class (one shared copy), and a `static` method has no `this`.

sections.title: Instance Members vs Static Members
sections.content:
| | Instance member | Static member |
|---|---|---|
| Declared with | No keyword | `static` keyword |
| Belongs to | Each individual object | The class itself |
| Memory | One copy per object | one value per loaded class |
| Access | `objectRef.field` | `ClassName.field` or `objectRef.field` |
| Can access `this`? | Yes | No — no object context |
| Can be called without object? | No | Yes |
| Use for | Data that varies per object | Shared data, utility methods, constants |
| Example | `name`, `marks`, `printGrade()` | `count`, `Math.abs()`, `Integer.parseInt()` |

sections.title: Static Counter — One Value Shared Across All Objects
Memory Layout — Instance Fields per Object, Static Field Shared
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Class["loaded Student class"] SF["static count = 3"] end subgraph Heap O1["s1 @ 0xA100
name: Alice
marks: 95"] O2["s2 @ 0xA200
name: Bob
marks: 72"] O3["s3 @ 0xA300
name: Carol
marks: 88"] end SF <-->|"shared — all objects
read & write same count"| O1 SF <-->|"shared"| O2 SF <-->|"shared"| O3 ``` `name` and `marks` are per-object — 3 objects = 3 copies. `count` is per-class — 3 objects, still just 1 copy.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making per-object data `static`** — declare `name` as `static` and suddenly every student shares one name, so the last object created silently overwrites everyone else's value.
- **Accessing instance fields from a static method** — a static method has no `this`, so referencing `name` or `marks` inside it is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
- **Reading static through an object reference** — `s1.count` compiles but misleads readers into thinking it's per-object; always use `Student.count` so it's clear the value belongs to the class.
- **Forgetting one static field is shared across all threads** — because instances of the same loaded class share that field, so two threads incrementing `count` at once can lose updates; shared static mutable state needs synchronization.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Instance fields** — each object gets its own copy. `s1.name` and `s2.name` are completely separate.
- **Static fields** — one copy per class, shared by every object. `Student.count` is the same number wherever you read it.
- **Static methods cannot access instance members** — no `this` means no object context; the compiler will reject it.
- **Access static via class name**, not object reference: `Student.count` is clearer than `s1.count` even though both work.
- **Common static uses**: counters, constants (`static final int MAX = 100`), utility methods (`Math.abs()`, `Integer.parseInt()`).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
It comes down to **ownership**. Instance members — anything without the `static` keyword — belong to each object, so every `Student` gets its own `name` and `marks`, and changing one student's doesn't touch another's. Static members belong to the class itself: there's exactly **one copy shared by everyone**, and you can use it without even creating an object, like `Student.count`.

The example I'd reach for is **a counter** — `static int count` with `count++` in the constructor — because it makes the shared nature obvious: every `new` bumps the same number, so the class knows how many objects exist.

The constraint worth naming is that a `static` method **can't directly touch instance fields**, because it runs without any object, so there's no `this` to say whose `name` you mean — that's a compile error, and it trips people up.

The deeper point is the **trap of overusing static**: the moment you make something shared mutable state, you've created one value that every object and every thread sees, which can quietly clobber data or race. So I keep `static` for genuinely class-wide things — counters, constants, utilities — and leave per-object data as instance fields.
